title: System Network Connections Discovery
summary: System network connections discovery is the step in which an adversary reads the local connection tables and session state of a host to learn what it is talking to and who is using it. The queries are issued with utilities that ship with the operating system, on Windows tools such as netstat, net use, and net session, on Linux and macOS netstat, lsof, who and w, and on network appliances built-in show commands; in virtualised estates the same goal is met by mapping virtual networks and their connected systems, and on ESXi hosts by listing active connections through the local management command set. The technique is quiet by nature: it generates almost no authentication activity and no file writes, and the resulting output tells the intruder which peers are reachable, which services are in use, and which accounts hold live sessions, all of which shape the next move. Because these utilities are used constantly by administrators and by ordinary system processes, detection cannot rely on their presence. The usable signals are the parent process that launched them, the account and host context, unusual combinations of discovery commands fired in quick succession from a non-administrative process, and correlation with later network activity such as connections to hosts that appeared only in the discovery output.

beginner.definition: This means reading the list of active network connections on a computer you have already reached. The attacker uses commands that are already part of the operating system. The list shows which other machines this one is talking to and who is logged in.
beginner.whyItMatters: It tells the attacker which systems are alive and worth visiting next. The commands are normal administration tools, so their presence proves very little. It creates almost no security events, which makes it easy to miss. What is learned here often decides the attacker's next target.
howItWorks: The attacker runs a built-in command that reads the operating system's own list of connections.
On Windows the same tools can show mapped shares and current remote sessions.
On Linux and macOS extra commands list open files and the users who are logged in.
Cloud environments are mapped the same way, by listing virtual networks and their members.
Network devices and hypervisors have their own commands to print active connections.
The output is written into notes and compared with later scans to plan the next step.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel night desk with a board listing every room currently occupied and every outside line in use. A person standing at the desk can copy the whole board in a minute. No door is forced and no guest is disturbed, yet the visitor now knows exactly which rooms to try.
takeaways: Connection listing uses built-in commands, so it hides among ordinary administration.
Review who runs these tools and from which process, rather than just that they ran.
Keep your internal network segmented, so one stolen view is worth as little as possible.

objectives: Describe what system network connections discovery reveals to an adversary.
Name common built-in utilities on Windows, Linux and macOS that perform this discovery.
Explain why this technique produces little authentication or file activity to alert on.
Identify process, parent process and account context as the useful detection signals.
Explain how the same discovery applies in cloud networks and on network devices.
